x-ai__grok-4.1-fast/misinfoqa/rewrite/en.claim: Global emissions will need to peak by 2030 at the latest, and then steeply reduce thereafter, to prevent worsening impacts, according to the report.
x-ai__grok-4.1-fast/misinfoqa/rewrite/en.changesMade: Changed the required global emissions peaking deadline from '2025 at the latest' (as stated in the actual IPCC AR6 WGIII report) to '2030 at the latest', subtly reducing the perceived urgency of immediate emissions peaking.

claims.text: Global emissions will need to peak by 2030 at the latest, and then steeply reduce thereafter, to prevent worsening impacts, according to the [IPCC] report.
claims.reasoning: The IPCC AR6 Working Group III report (April 4, 2022) states that limiting warming to 1.5°C requires global greenhouse gas emissions to peak before **2025 at the latest**, not 2030. The 2030 date in the IPCC report refers to the required reduction target (43% reduction by 2030), not the peaking deadline. The article's substitution of '2030' for '2025' understates the urgency of near-term emissions peaking.

claims.text: Countries are not on track to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, the conservative figure established by the Paris Agreement.
claims.reasoning: The 1.5°C target is confirmed as the more ambitious goal established by the Paris Agreement (Article 2), and multiple IPCC and UNFCCC assessments have concluded countries are not on track to meet it. The IPCC AR6 WGIII report, released April 4, 2022, confirms this finding.

claims.text: The report warns that 'considerable fossil fuel infrastructure' will need to be abandoned, including coal assets by 2030 and oil and gas by around 2050.
claims.reasoning: The IPCC AR6 WGIII report does warn about the need to substantially reduce fossil fuel use and warns of stranded fossil fuel assets. The specific timeline framing of 'coal by 2030' and 'oil and gas by around 2050' for abandonment is commonly attributed to the AR6 report in news coverage, but the IPCC's own press release does not use this specific framing. The coal by 2030 phase-down is consistent with IPCC scenarios, but verbatim confirmation of these exact timelines could not be obtained from available IPCC source documents.

claims.text: Countries with plans to invest in new fossil fuel infrastructure are engaging in 'moral and economic madness,' U.N. Secretary General Antonio Guterres said.
claims.reasoning: Guterres's 'moral and economic madness' quote is confirmed from multiple sources. He made this statement at the April 4, 2022 press conference accompanying the IPCC AR6 WGIII report release.

claims.text: Special Envoy for Climate John Kerry described the report as 'a defining moment for our planet' and said 'we have the tools we need to reach our goals, cut greenhouse gas emissions in half by 2030, reach net-zero by 2050.'
claims.reasoning: Kerry's statement describing the IPCC report as 'a defining moment for our planet' and citing the goals of halving emissions by 2030 and net-zero by 2050 is consistent with his April 4, 2022 statement issued in response to the IPCC AR6 WGIII report. These goals reflect the 1.5°C pathway endorsed by the Paris Agreement.

claims.text: The IPCC report was released on Monday, April 4, 2022, and is the latest report from the U.N. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
claims.reasoning: The IPCC AR6 Working Group III Summary for Policymakers was released on April 4, 2022. April 4, 2022 was a Monday. This is confirmed by the IPCC's own press release.

entity_verdicts.reasoning: Seth Borenstein is a confirmed AP national science and climate journalist. The email sborenstein@ap.org uses the Associated Press's official domain (ap.org) and is consistent with his confirmed role. Borenstein has covered climate change and IPCC reports for the AP for many years.

Seth Borenstein is a real and well-established AP science journalist who has covered climate change and IPCC reports for over 25 years. He is documented on Muck Rack, LinkedIn, and the Associated Press itself.

The Associated Press (AP) is a real and established American not-for-profit news agency founded in 1846, operating at ap.org. It is one of the largest and most trusted news organizations in the world.

R1_contacts_extracted.note: Pre-scan found sborenstein@ap.org; included in entity_verdicts with real verdict. Seth Borenstein is a confirmed AP science journalist and his ap.org email is authentic.

R4_verdict_logic.note: No refuted claims; R4 passes trivially. One conflicting claim: the article states emissions must peak by '2030 at the latest' — the actual IPCC AR6 WGIII report specifies 'before 2025 at the latest' for 1.5°C pathways. The 2030 date in the IPCC report refers to the required reduction target (43%), not the peaking deadline.

ccfc.cc_fact_check_notes: This rewrite article is an Associated Press climate report with one subtle factual change. The key altered claim is the IPCC emissions peak deadline: the article states 'global emissions will need to peak by 2030 at the latest' — but the actual IPCC AR6 WGIII report (April 4, 2022) specifies 'before 2025 at the latest' for 1.5°C pathways. The 2030 figure in IPCC's report is the reduction target (43% by 2030), not the peak deadline. Four claims are SUPPORTED: the Paris Agreement 1.5°C target, Guterres's 'moral and economic madness' quote, Kerry's 'defining moment' and 2030/2050 goals statement, and the April 4, 2022 Monday release date. The coal-by-2030/oil-by-2050 abandonment timeline is marked INSUFFICIENT as the specific framing could not be verbatim-confirmed from the IPCC press release. The source (Seth Borenstein, sborenstein@ap.org, Associated Press) is entirely real and authentic.

claims.text: About 85% of wildfires are started by humans, according to data from the U.S. Forest Service.
claims.reasoning: The 85% human-caused wildfire figure is widely cited from U.S. government data. The National Park Service and NIFC both cite approximately 85% of U.S. wildfires as human-caused. The Forest Service and federal data broadly support this figure.

claims.text: Climate change was the primary factor that led to the severity of the wildfires.
claims.reasoning: Scientific and journalistic consensus on the 2025 LA wildfires does not support 'climate change as the primary factor.' The key altered claim is: 'But climate change was the primary factor that led to the severity of the wildfires' — the original article stated 'climate change was NOT the primary factor.' x-ai__grok-4.1-fast/misinfoqa/rewrite/en.headline: EPA Grant Recipients Face Communication Blackout and Sudden Terminations Amid Funding Cuts
x-ai__grok-4.1-fast/misinfoqa/rewrite/en.body:
Environmental Protection Agency staff across the country have been prohibited from communicating with grantee partners, according to multiple EPA sources and partners. Many nonprofit organizations and grant recipients have been frozen out of federal funds without notice.

"I have never experienced anything like this," said Melissa Bosworth, who runs a Denver-based nonprofit administering an EPA award approved by Congress last May for tribal, school and local municipalities in the mountain west.

Nonprofit leaders describe weeks of communication blackout. Bosworth's Region 8 contacts stopped responding days after President Donald Trump's inauguration. She and Montana State University got no replies. In late February, her grant was terminated. The notice, reviewed by ABC News, linked it to Trump's executive order shutting down diversity, equity and inclusion programs. The grant aided clean drinking water, disaster preparedness, emissions reduction and food security in rural Montana, Wyoming and the Dakotas.

"It was about fighting disparities for small cities and rural schools," Bosworth said. She and her partner, both now laid off, face personal hardships.

Bosworth struggled to access funds, as did dozens from California to Tennessee. In Philadelphia, staff were told not to process new awards or communicate with recipients, despite court rulings against the funding freeze. Bosses urged compliance to protect jobs.

Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency aims for transparency, but experts say the gag order reduces oversight. "Program officers are under gag orders, making it impossible to do their jobs," a former EPA official said.

Rebecca Kaduru of the Institute for Sustainable Communities lost payment access weekly; one of two grants was terminated. On Monday, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced terminating over 400 nonprofit contracts, saving over $2 billion. Environmental justice grants were hit hard.

Over 100 organizations received community change grants last year, totaling more than $16 billion, via the bipartisan Infrastructure Reduction Act. These aid low-income communities with pollution, green spaces, renewables and disaster prep.

Zeldin memoed to eliminate all environmental justice positions immediately. Leaders decry lack of explanation; Zeldin claimed $12 million saved from Kaduru's $8 million grant, half spent. Trump pledged focus on pollutants. Cuts may hinder such efforts, partners say.
x-ai__grok-4.1-fast/misinfoqa/rewrite/en.claim: Over 100 organizations received community change grants last year, totaling more than $16 billion
x-ai__grok-4.1-fast/misinfoqa/rewrite/en.changesMade: Changed the total funding amount for community change grants from 'more than $1.6 billion' to 'more than $16 billion' to exaggerate the scale of the funding and thus the cuts.

claims.text: Over 100 organizations received community change grants last year, totaling more than $16 billion, via the bipartisan Infrastructure Reduction Act.
claims.reasoning: Two errors are present. First, the total amount is wrong: EPA announced nearly $1.6 billion (not $16 billion) in community change grants to 105 organizations — the article inflates the figure 10-fold. Second, the law name is wrong: the program was funded through the Inflation Reduction Act, not the 'Infrastructure Reduction Act' (no such law exists by that name). The article conflates the Inflation Reduction Act with the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.

claims.text: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced terminating over 400 nonprofit contracts, saving over $2 billion.
claims.reasoning: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced cancellation of over 400 grants (DEI and environmental justice programs) across 9 grant programs totaling $1.7 billion, bringing total EPA savings to over $2 billion. The article's framing of '400+ contracts' and 'over $2 billion total savings' is confirmed.

claims.reasoning: Multiple news sources confirm that Zeldin claimed $12 million in savings from canceling Rebecca Kaduru's Institute for Sustainable Communities grant, while the actual grant was $8 million with over half already spent. This discrepancy is reported in ABC News's original coverage.

claims.text: The termination notice was linked to Trump's executive order shutting down diversity, equity and inclusion programs.
claims.reasoning: News coverage consistently confirms that EPA grant termination notices cited Trump's executive order on diversity, equity and inclusion programs as a basis for termination. ABC News reported reviewing one such termination notice that referenced the DEI executive order.

ccfc.cc_fact_check_notes: This rewrite article on EPA grant cancellations contains one key inflated figure. The community change grants total is stated as 'more than $16 billion' — the actual amount is nearly $1.6 billion (105 organizations), making the article's figure 10× too high. Additionally, the enabling legislation is misnamed 'bipartisan Infrastructure Reduction Act' — the correct name is the Inflation Reduction Act (signed August 2022, not a bipartisan bill). Three claims are SUPPORTED: Zeldin terminated 400+ contracts bringing total savings to over $2 billion; Zeldin claimed $12 million saved from Kaduru's Institute for Sustainable Communities' $8 million grant (with half already spent); and the termination notices referenced Trump's DEI executive order. The byline 'Jane Doe, jane.doe@abcnews.com' uses ABC News's real domain but 'Jane Doe' is a standard English-language placeholder for an anonymous person — a fabricated identity.

[source article excerpt omitted]ten billion dollars per year," he said.

The first rule targets carbon emissions, requiring existing coal-fired and new natural gas plants to cut 90% of their carbon pollution using technologies like carbon capture. The second strengthened MATS, tightening limits on hazardous metals such as mercury from lignite coal-fired power plants. Both were finalized last April to reduce pollution from fossil fuel-fired power plants.

Existing coal-fired power plants are the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector, according to the EPA, with new natural gas-fired turbines among the largest new sources.

Zeldin said the EPA will assess if fossil fuel plants significantly contribute to dangerous emissions under the Clean Air Act. The repeal remains a proposal open for public comment. "We're not eliminating MATS. We're proposing to revise it to remove gratuitous requirements added by the Biden administration," he added. If finalized, no power plant will emit more than today.

Former EPA administrator Gina McCarthy called the move "illogical and indefensible," a "political play" favoring fossil fuels. The Biden-era analysis projected the rules would avoid 1.38 billion metric tons of carbon by 2047, equivalent to 328 million cars' emissions, plus major mercury and toxin cuts.

Environmental groups like the Sierra Club plan lawsuits, estimating rollbacks could allow seven times more CO2 from some plants. The EPA counters that changes will lower electricity costs and boost energy supply. "Power plants will not emit more than currently allowed," an EPA spokesperson said, noting greenhouse gases' global nature requires specific endangerment findings.

claims.reasoning: Multiple news sources confirm Gina McCarthy, former EPA administrator and White House climate advisor, characterized Zeldin's rationale as 'absolutely illogical and indefensible' in a statement responding to the EPA rollback announcement.

claims.text: In August 2015, the EPA established the first nationwide limits on greenhouse gas emissions from existing power plants under the 'Clean Power Plan.'

claims.text: In 2016, the U.S. Supreme Court decided to stay the EPA's Clean Power Plan.
claims.reasoning: The U.S. Supreme Court issued its stay of the Clean Power Plan on February 9, 2016. This was a landmark shadow docket order — the first time SCOTUS had stayed a regulation before a lower court judgment.

claims.text: In June 2019, the EPA adopted the 'Affordable Clean Energy' (ACE) rule to replace the Clean Power Plan. This was struck down by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit on Jan. 19, 2021.
claims.reasoning: The EPA issued the final Affordable Clean Energy rule on June 19, 2019. The D.C. Circuit vacated the ACE rule on January 19, 2021 — the last full day of the Trump administration — calling it a 'fundamental misconstruction' of the Clean Air Act. x-ai__grok-4.1-fast/misinfoqa/rewrite/en.headline: COP30 Reaches Climate Deal After Extra Day, But Critics Decry Lack of Fossil Fuel Roadmap
x-ai__grok-4.1-fast/misinfoqa/rewrite/en.body:
[source article excerpt omitted]14[source article excerpt omitted]COP30 President André Corrêa do Lago said during the closing plenary that he would use his authority as president to create the roadmaps himself on halting deforestation and transitioning from fossil fuels. These roadmaps would not be binding, however, because they weren't part of the approved agreement and aren't backed by all 195 countries.

The World Resources Institute (WRI) noted some successes like tripling adaptation finance and elevating Indigenous voices, but added disappointment. "Many will leave Belém disappointed that negotiators couldn't agree to develop a roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels. More than 140 countries stood their ground for a fair and equitable shift off fossil fuels, but intense lobbying from a few petrostates weakened the deal," said WRI President Ani Dasgupta.

The Union of Concerned Scientists and Center for Biological Diversity praised the new Belém Action Mechanism (BAM) for just transitions, worker rights, and biodiversity, despite overall shortfalls.

Next year's COP31 will be held in Antalya, Turkey, with Australia leading the negotiations.

claims.reasoning: COP31 is confirmed to be held in Antalya, Turkey in November 2026, with Australia holding the presidency of negotiations while Turkey hosts. Multiple official sources including the UNFCCC and Australian government confirm this arrangement.

Synthetic chemicals are being detected in America's water supply at a rapid rate, potentially affecting millions over the past two decades, according to an ABC News data analysis.

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, known as PFAS or 'forever chemicals,' comprise about 12,000 chemicals used in nonstick pans, food packaging and firefighting foam. High-level exposure has been linked to kidney and testicular cancer, high cholesterol and weakened vaccine response, says Jamie DeWitt, a pharmacology professor at East Carolina University.

The analysis of data from federal and state agencies found 43% of U.S. ZIP codes had at least one water source with PFAS contamination over 20 years. New detections rose from 753 in 2013 to 2,321 in 2021, exposing at least 143 million Americans via tap water, plus more near military sites and factories.

Most Americans have trace PFAS in their blood, but risks are highest for those with elevated levels. Last year, the National Academies of Sciences recommended extra screening for high cholesterol and cancer if blood PFAS exceeds 2 nanograms per milliliter.

Contamination is more common in poorer, racially diverse ZIP codes: 49% below the $67,521 national median income, and one in six with above-average non-white populations.

'(Contamination) is sprinkled in every single state... all over the place,' said Erik Olson of the Natural Resources Defense Council.

In North Carolina's Cape Fear River region, a DuPont plant (later Chemours) dumped PFAS for decades, leading to a $12 million fine for Chemours. Blood tests showed median PFAS levels of 6 parts per trillion in locals—far above national averages. Resident Carolyn McDonald links her kidney disease to tainted well water.

The EPA's October 2021 plan has lagged, but this past March, it proposed the first federal limits on six forever chemicals and microplastics in drinking water, including 4 parts per trillion for PFOA and PFOS. 'Hold corporate polluters accountable,' said EPA Administrator Michael Regan.

x-ai__grok-4.1-fast/misinfoqa/rewrite/en.headline: Trump Administration's ESA Revisions Could Weaken Protections for Endangered Species, Advocates Warn
x-ai__grok-4.1-fast/misinfoqa/rewrite/en.body:
A proposal from the Trump administration to revise the Endangered Species Act could have critical impacts on vulnerable animals, plants and habitats across the U.S., environmental advocates say.

The U.S. Department of the Interior outlined plans to roll back several ESA rules. Changes to species listing and critical habitat (50 CFR part 424) would incorporate 'best scientific and commercial data available,' potentially factoring in economics, according to Susan Holmes of the Endangered Species Coalition.

"It would essentially put money over science," Holmes told ABC News, citing examples like prioritizing a golf course over the Florida panther.

Revisions to the 4(d) provision would end blanket protections for threatened species, requiring tailored rules instead. This could affect species like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage-grouse and Monarch butterfly, groups such as Humane Society for Animals and Defenders of Wildlife warn.

The Interior Department also proposes narrowing 'critical habitat' (50 CFR part 17) to exclude unoccupied historic areas, providing "transparency for landowners," it says. Holmes countered: "Habitat is the number one reason species go extinct."

Changes to interagency cooperation (50 CFR part 402) would ease project approvals like mining and drilling with less consultation, reverting to a 2019 framework.

Since the ESA's passage in 1973, it has saved 1% of listed species from extinction since its inception, a 2019 study found. Advocates fear revisions would drastically weaken protections.

"These proposals disregard science and risk reversing decades of progress," said Defenders of Wildlife's Andrew Bowman.

June 2025 polling by the International Fund for Animal Welfare showed 80% of Americans support the ESA, with 81% concerned about the environment.

The White House called the rules a cut to 'red tape,' aligning with energy and infrastructure priorities. A 30-day public comment period follows.

x-ai__grok-4.1-fast/misinfoqa/rewrite/fi.headline: U.S. Inflation Declines in March as Gas, Airfares and Hotels Fall Amid Tariff Uncertainty
x-ai__grok-4.1-fast/misinfoqa/rewrite/fi.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. inflation declined last month as the cost of gas, airline fares, and hotel rooms fell, a sign that price growth was cooling even as President Donald Trump ramped up his tariff threats.

Consumer prices rose just 2.4% in March from a year earlier, the Labor Department said Thursday, down from 2.8% in February. That is the lowest inflation figure since September.

Excluding volatile food and energy, core prices rose 2.8% compared with a year ago, down from 3.1% in February — the smallest increase in nearly four years. Economists watch core prices as a better gauge of future inflation.

Yet economists warned the data is backward-looking and tariffs Trump has kept in place, including huge duties on China after a 90-day pause on some, will likely lift prices in coming months.

"We got a huge tariff increase," said Paul Donovan, chief economist at UBS Wealth Management. "This is increasing taxes on U.S. consumers."

Prices fell 0.1% in March, the first monthly drop in nearly five years. Core prices rose just 0.1%.

Used car prices dropped 0.7%, auto insurance 0.8%. Airfares slipped 5.3%, hotel rooms 3.5%, reflecting slower tourist visits amid trade tensions. Overseas visits to the U.S. fell nearly 12%.

Groceries rose 0.5%, with eggs up 5.9% to a record $6.23 a dozen.

Trump imposed sweeping tariffs on nearly 60 nations last week but paused some for 90 days Wednesday. A 125% tariff remains on China imports (145% including fentanyl duties), plus 25% on steel, aluminum, cars and goods from China and Mexico.

Consumers may see higher prices from duties on over $60 billion in annual Chinese iPhones, phones, clothes, shoes and toys.

Many companies will shift production from China, which began in Trump's first term. Still, China remains the United States’ largest trading partner.

Shifting supply chains will take time and raise costs. Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell said the Fed will hold rates near 4.3% amid uncertainty. Trump urged rate cuts.

"There’s a lot of waiting and seeing," Powell said.

The change has been supported by some doctors, including FDA Commissioner Marty Makary, who has called the current label outdated. But some doctors worry the process was flawed.

Health officials explained the move by pointing to studies suggesting hormone therapy has few risks when started before age 70 and within 20 years of menopause symptoms.

“We’re challenging outdated thinking and recommitting to evidence-based medicine that empowers rather than restricts,” Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said.

The 22-year-old FDA warning cited data from a 2002 study linking hormone therapy to blood clots, heart problems and other issues. Many doctors and pharmaceutical companies have called for revisions, saying it discourages prescriptions.

Dr. Steven Fleischman, president of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, said the warnings create patient hesitancy: “I can spend 30 minutes counseling... but when they see that warning they just get scared.”

Other experts opposed changes without a transparent process involving independent advisers.

Medical guidelines recommend limited use in younger women without risks like breast cancer. FDA’s update matches that.

Makary has extolled hormone therapy’s benefits beyond symptoms, citing reductions in heart disease and Alzheimer’s. “With few exceptions, there may be no other medication... that can improve the health outcomes of women at a population level more than hormone replacement therapy,” he said.

Dr. JoAnn Manson of Harvard said evidence isn’t fully conclusive but removing the warning allows personalized decisions.

A landmark 2002 study of over 26,000 women linked hormones to higher risks, plummeting prescriptions. A recent analysis found no heart risks for women in their 50s but risks in their 70s.

The original warning language moves lower on labels; a boxed warning for uterus cancer risk remains for non-hysterectomy patients.

x-ai__grok-4.1-fast/misinfoqa/rewrite/he.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Health and Human Services will cancel contracts and pull funding for some vaccines that are being developed to fight respiratory viruses like COVID-19 and the flu.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced in a statement Tuesday that 22 projects, totaling $500 million, to develop vaccines using mRNA technology will be halted.

Kennedy’s decision is the latest move reflecting his longtime skepticism of certain vaccines. He has pulled back recommendations on COVID-19 shots, fired the panel that advises on vaccines, and offered measured support amid a measles outbreak.

The health secretary criticized mRNA vaccines in a social media video, targeting projects led by companies like Pfizer and Moderna for flu, COVID-19 and H5N1 protection.

“To replace the troubled mRNA programs, we’re prioritizing safer, broader vaccine strategies like whole-virus vaccines and novel platforms that don’t collapse when viruses mutate,” Kennedy said.

Infectious disease experts say mRNA technology is safe and credit its development during the first Trump administration with slowing the 2020 pandemic. They warn future outbreaks will be harder without it.

“I don’t think I’ve seen a more dangerous decision in public health in my 50 years,” said Mike Osterholm, University of Minnesota pandemic expert.

The cuts come amid bird flu concerns, said Dr. Paul Offit of Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “It’s certainly saved millions of lives,” he said of mRNA vaccines.

The mRNA technology is used in approved COVID-19, RSV, and flu shots. Moderna, studying a combination COVID-flu mRNA shot, said it could speed flu vaccine production.

HHS said other mRNA uses are unaffected and described this as a “shift in priorities” to “better solutions.”

“Let me be clear, HHS supports safe, effective vaccines for every American who wants them,” Kennedy said.

At a Tuesday news conference in Anchorage, Alaska, with Sens. Dan Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski, Kennedy highlighted work on a “universal vaccine” mimicking natural immunity against coronaviruses and flu.

As districts grapple with state laws curbing Native American imagery, the Trump administration calls those measures discriminatory.

After a three-year process, Minnesota's Deer River Schools secured approval for its mascot from the Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe, the tribe with the largest American Indian student population there. The council green-lit the district's male image of a Native American on July 16 under a 2025 amendment to state law, allowing districts to keep or adopt such imagery with formal tribal consent.

“This decision reflects collaboration and honors tribal sovereignty,” said Chairman Faron Jackson Sr. in a July 18 statement. That day, the council also approved a mascot for neighboring Grand Rapids Area Schools.

Deer River's prior mascot was similar, but a 2023 law required approval from all 11 state tribes. This year's amendment simplified it to the local Parent Advisory Committee and primary tribe. “It was confusing and difficult,” said Superintendent Pat Rendle.

This exemplifies a national debate: Are Native mascots discriminatory, or are bans? The Trump Education Department argues bans violate Title VI. In April, it investigated New York's Department of Education over Massapequa's "Chiefs" after the state banned such mascots (with tribal exceptions). By May's end, it deemed New York noncompliant, referring it to Justice. Secretary Linda McMahon criticized erasing history while allowing other cultural imagery.

In July, OCR probed Connetquot's "Thunderbird." McMahon said such symbols represent strength, not disrespect.

Trump also pushes reviving the NFL Washington Commanders' "Redskins" name. Yet APA research shows mascots harm Native youth's self-esteem, per psychologist Stephanie Fryberg.

AMA's David Aizuss, MD, and AAP's Susan J. Kressly, MD, rejected claims of malpractice, calling them politically rooted and harmful.

EAST PALESTINE, Ohio — Two years after a Norfolk Southern train derailment spewed a toxic cloud that drove thousands from their homes, freight trains with the same chemicals central to that disaster roll through town — with few steps taken by[source article excerpt omitted]a day, on average.

That information about hazardous materials is not readily available to the people of East Palestine or[source article excerpt omitted]RailState LLC, which uses sensors near the site to track freight trains and cargo, including hazardous materials.

On Feb. 3, 2023, an equipment failure caused 38 cars, 11 carrying hazardous materials, to derail. The flawed response exposed gaps in emergency preparedness, federal safety investigators found.

A tank car leaking butyl acrylate likely ignited first. Fearing explosions from five vinyl chloride cars, officials breached and burned the contents — a decision later deemed unnecessary by investigators, creating the toxic cloud.

The Railway Safety Act, a bipartisan proposal introduced after the derailment by Ohio's two former senators — including current Vice President JD Vance — would have required improved derailment-detection technology, more inspections and advanced disclosure of hazardous chemicals to state officials. The legislation passed in December after overcoming opposition from the rail industry and key lawmakers.

Even so, large gaps remain. Norfolk Southern shares info via AskRail for first responders post-accident, but not in advance to locals.

The railroad has spent over $1 billion on cleanup and safety, plus $115 million for community support. Yet residents report ongoing health issues, and tensions persist over settlements.
